title: Mastery of the elements (3.44–3.46)
hook: samyama on the five elements brings the classic eight powers and a perfected body, and the commentary adds who doesn't use them to rearrange the world

segments.voice: Yesterday: entering another body, and your line, read as the tradition reads it. Mind and body, both of nature. Did a strange story make more sense from the inside? Day four hundred seventy-five.

In the Ramayana, Hanuman has to cross the ocean to find Sita. He grows enormous, a mountain of a monkey, and leaps. When he lands near the golden city of Lanka, he needs the opposite. So he shrinks, small enough to slip past the guards at nightfall. Vast when the task is vast. Tiny when the task is tiny. The Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn sung in homes and temples, calls him the giver of the eight powers. Today Patanjali names where those eight come from, and adds a list for the body that sounds like a blessing.
screen: `HANUMAN GROWS VAST.` → `THEN SMALL ENOUGH TO SLIP IN.` → `THE EIGHT POWERS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.44: by samyama on the elements in five aspects, mastery of the elements. Bhuta-jaya. The elements are the five of Indian thought: earth, water, fire, air, space. And Patanjali looks at each one five ways: its gross form, its essential nature, its subtle root, how it's woven of the three qualities, and what it's for. Earth's essential nature, says the commentary, is its solidity. Water's, its wetness. Fire's, its heat. Air's, its movement. Space's, that it's everywhere. Sutra 3.45: from this mastery comes minuteness and the rest, the perfection of the body, and freedom from being blocked by the elements. The commentary lists the eight: becoming tiny, becoming light, becoming vast, reaching anything, getting what one wills, control, lordship, and fulfilling one's resolve. The eight of the hymn. Sutra 3.46 says what the perfected body is: beauty, grace, strength, and a hardness like a diamond. Today's line: the body's perfection. Then the commentary adds a line worth remembering. Even though such a yogi could, they don't overturn the order of things, because that order was set by the will of one perfected long before. Later commentators name that one Ishvara. Total mastery, and the master leaves the world's order alone. And remember where this list sits: right after 3.37, the warning. Even a diamond body is an obstacle in samadhi.
screen: `BHUTA-JAYA: MASTERY OF ELEMENTS.` · `EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR, SPACE.` · `TINY, LIGHT, VAST: THE EIGHT.` · `BEAUTY, GRACE, STRENGTH, DIAMOND.` · then, large: `THE BODY'S PERFECTION.`

segments.voice: Today's practice greets the five elements in your own body. Sit steady and easy. Feel earth: the weight of you on the seat. Feel water: the moisture in your mouth. Feel fire: the warmth in your hands. Feel air: the breath moving in and out. Feel space: the room around you, and the space inside the chest. Spend a few breaths with each, then rest in all five at once. The bell holds the time.
Mastery of the elements. Bhuta-jaya, which brings the eight powers and the body's perfection: beauty, grace, strength and diamond hardness.
Your line: the body's perfection. Today, when you could bend a situation your way just because you can, try leaving its order alone once, and see what happens. Day four hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Hanuman as the giver of the eight siddhis, and the Hanuman Chalisa is widely sung; in the Yoga tradition, the eight powers of 3.45 are understood as fruits of mastery that a practitioner is warned not to pursue for their own sake.

fork.setup: you've mastered the elements. you could change how fire and water behave for everyone. what does the commentary say such a yogi does?
options: rearranges the world to suit them.
leaves the order of things as it is.
uses it only to win arguments.
fork.reveal: the commentary on 3.45: though capable, the yogi doesn't overturn the order of things, because it was willed by one perfected long before.

original.note: Sanskrit bhūta-jaya: victory over, mastery of (jaya) the elements (bhūta), 3.44.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga promises a perfect body.
what it means: samyama on the elements brings the eight powers and a perfected body, still an obstacle to samadhi.
what a scholar hears: five aspects in 3.44 (sthula, svarupa, sukshma, anvaya, arthavattva); anima and the rest in 3.45; rupa, lavanya, bala and vajra-samhananatva in 3.46.

notes: Bhashya on 3.44: the essential natures (murti/solidity, sneha/wetness, ushnata/heat, pranami/movement, sarvatogati/omnipresence): confirm renderings.
The eight siddhis as listed in the Bhashya on 3.45 (anima, laghima, mahima, prapti, prakamya, vashitva, ishitritva, yatrakamavasayitva): confirm.
Bhashya on 3.45 that the yogi, though capable, does not reverse the order of things, set by the will of the primordially perfected one: confirm.
Hanuman's small form when entering Lanka (often 'the size of a cat' in Valmiki); kept as 'small enough to slip past the guards'. The Chalisa line (ashta siddhi nau nidhi ke data) is paraphrased.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'millions of Hindus' count and named the Hanuman Chalisa as the source (added to sources); the Bhashya on 3.45 says 'one perfected before' (purva-siddha), and identifying that one as Ishvara is now credited to later commentators (teach, myth, fork). Keeper: confirm Vachaspati Mishra's identification.
